claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC phase.
The range of phases observed in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 originates from short-range chemical ordering developed during cooling and thermal exposure.
Short-range chemical order acts as a precursor to secondary-phase nucleation.
Element-specific differences in diffusivity and mixing enthalpy foster local chemical segregation during cooling.
Al-rich clusters develop in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 during cooling or thermal exposure.
Local chemical segregation destabilizes the initial BCC phase in favor of FCC or B2 structures.
Rapid quenching limits short-range-order development, whereas slow cooling or intermediate-temperature annealing permits it to evolve.
The proposed mechanism applies when cooling rates and annealing times permit sufficient atomic diffusion and SRO formation.
Sufficiently rapid cooling freezes diffusion and suppresses the proposed ordering mechanism.
At temperatures where BCC is the equilibrium phase irrespective of ordering, the proposed mechanism does not apply.
Ordered clustering locally lowers the free-energy barrier for nucleation of secondary phases.
A rapidly quenched sample will largely retain BCC and show minimal secondary-phase precipitation.
Slow cooling or annealing will increase secondary-phase fractions relative to rapid quenching.
Longer cooling times or intermediate-temperature exposures will produce new diffraction peaks attributable to FCC or ordered B2 phases.
The rapidly quenched baseline maintains the high-temperature BCC structure with limited SRO.
External stress or impurities can override diffusion-controlled ordering and make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
